# Capstone Part 1: Design and Build a Production AI System

##### The portfolio project that got the offer

Two candidates interviewed for the same senior AI engineer role in Bengaluru.

The first showed six notebooks: a Titanic classifier, an MNIST CNN, a sentiment model, a churn predictor, a small RAG demo, a fine-tuned LLM. Each was competent. The interview lasted forty minutes and covered surface area.

The second showed one project: a warranty-claim triage system for an appliance manufacturer. Fourteen thousand real claims scraped from a public complaints portal, OCR over attached invoices, a classifier for claim category, a RAG layer over warranty policy documents, and a fraud flag. She brought a design document with a latency budget, an evaluation report with per-slice metrics and confidence intervals, an MLflow registry showing eleven tracked runs, and a section titled "what I got wrong and how I found out."

The interview ran ninety minutes and never left that project. She got the offer.

**Breadth is a beginner signal. One system, taken to production depth, is a senior signal.** The next two days build that system. Today is design, data and model; tomorrow is deployment and operations.

##### Choosing a project that will hold up

Four criteria, and the third is the one people skip:

1. **You can obtain real, messy data.** Kaggle-clean data lets you skip the work that demonstrates competence.
2. **There is a plausible business metric**, not just an accuracy number.
3. **It has at least one genuinely hard component** — a real latency constraint, an imbalance problem, a multimodal input, an operational requirement.
4. **You can explain it in ninety seconds** to someone non-technical.

Ideas that satisfy all four, using data you can actually get in India:

| Project | Data source | Hard part |
|---|---|---|
| Consumer-complaint triage and routing | Public grievance portals | Multilingual, class imbalance, OCR attachments |
| Mandi price forecasting with anomaly alerts | Agmarknet open data | Time-series, missing data, drift by season |
| Legal-clause QA over contract templates | Public tenders, standard-form contracts | Long documents, citation, precision requirement |
| Transit delay prediction | GTFS + open transit feeds | Streaming features, real-time serving |
| Medical-report structuring | Synthetic + de-identified samples | PII, structured extraction, safety |
| Job-posting deduplication and skill extraction | Scraped listings | Entity resolution at scale, embeddings |

Scope ruthlessly. One model or one RAG pipeline, one clearly-stated user, one primary metric. A capstone that tries to be a platform ends up being a README.

##### The design document

Write this before any code. It is the artifact interviewers read first and the discipline that prevents six weeks of drift.

```markdown
# Warranty Claim Triage — Design Document
Author: ... | Date: 2026-07-28 | Status: Draft

## 1. Problem
Service centres receive ~800 warranty claims/day. Manual triage takes a
technician 6 minutes per claim and misroutes ~18%, causing an average 3.2-day
SLA breach. Misrouting costs ~₹340/claim in rework.

## 2. Goals / Non-goals
Goals:
  - Auto-classify claims into 9 categories with per-category precision >= 0.85
  - Flag likely-fraudulent claims for review (top 5% by score)
  - Answer technician policy questions with page-level citations
Non-goals:
  - Auto-approving or rejecting claims (human decides — deliberate)
  - Real-time streaming ingestion (daily batch is sufficient)
  - Regional-language support beyond English and Hindi in v1

## 3. Success metrics
Primary (business): misroute rate 18% -> under 8%
Model: macro-F1 >= 0.82; worst-category precision >= 0.75
Guardrails: p95 latency < 900 ms; cost < ₹0.40/claim; zero PII in logs

## 4. Users and constraints
Users: 140 service-centre coordinators, desktop, office network
Volume: 800/day now, 2,500/day projected in 12 months
Compliance: DPDP — claims contain names, phone numbers, addresses

## 5. Data
Source: 14,200 historical claims (2024-01 to 2026-05) + 1,100 policy PDF pages
Labels: existing routing decisions (NOTE: contains the 18% error — see risks)
Split: temporal — train to 2026-02, val 2026-03/04, test 2026-05

## 6. Approach
Baseline: TF-IDF + logistic regression (must beat this to justify anything else)
V1: fine-tuned multilingual encoder for classification; LightGBM for fraud
V2 (if needed): hybrid RAG over policy docs for the QA component

## 7. Evaluation plan
Temporal holdout; per-category and per-region slices; bootstrap CIs;
manual review of 100 errors before declaring done.

## 8. Risks
R1: Labels encode the 18% historical misroute rate.
    Mitigation: hand-relabel a 400-claim gold set; report on that too.
R2: Class imbalance — 3 categories are under 2% of volume.
    Mitigation: class weights, per-class thresholds, report macro not micro.
R3: OCR quality on photographed invoices.
    Mitigation: measure OCR CER on 50 samples before committing to that feature.

## 9. Milestones
W1 data + baseline | W2 model + eval | W3 serving + CI | W4 monitoring + docs
```

The **Non-goals** and **Risks** sections are what make this read as senior work. Anyone can list what they will build; stating what you deliberately will not build, and what you expect to go wrong, demonstrates judgement.

Risk R1 in that example is the genuinely interesting one — training on labels that contain an 18% error rate, and knowing it. Addressing that honestly (a hand-labelled gold set) is worth more in an interview than any modelling choice.

##### The data pipeline

```python
from prefect import flow, task
import pandera.pandas as pa
from pandera.typing import Series
import pandas as pd, hashlib

class ClaimSchema(pa.DataFrameModel):
    claim_id: Series[str] = pa.Field(unique=True)
    submitted_at: Series[pd.Timestamp]
    product_code: Series[str] = pa.Field(str_matches=r"^[A-Z]{2}\d{4}$")
    description: Series[str] = pa.Field(str_length={"min_value": 10})
    claim_amount_inr: Series[float] = pa.Field(ge=0, le=500_000)
    category: Series[str] = pa.Field(isin=CATEGORIES, nullable=True)

    class Config:
        strict = "filter"

@task(retries=2)
def ingest(as_of: str) -> str:
    df = fetch_claims(until=as_of)
    path = f"data/snapshots/dt={as_of}/claims.parquet"
    df.to_parquet(path, compression="zstd")
    return path

@task
def validate_and_clean(path: str) -> tuple[str, dict]:
    df = pd.read_parquet(path)
    n0 = len(df)
    try:
        ClaimSchema.validate(df, lazy=True)
    except pa.errors.SchemaErrors as e:
        bad = df.loc[e.failure_cases["index"].dropna().unique()]
        bad.to_parquet(path.replace("claims", "quarantine"))   # never drop silently
        df = df.drop(index=bad.index)
    df = redact_pii(df, cols=["description", "customer_name", "phone"])   # DPDP
    stats = {"in": n0, "out": len(df), "quarantined": n0 - len(df)}
    out = path.replace("claims", "clean")
    df.to_parquet(out)
    return out, stats

@task
def build_features(path: str, spec_version: str) -> str:
    df = pd.read_parquet(path)
    df = df.sort_values("submitted_at")
    # Leakage-safe: every aggregate uses only prior claims
    g = df.groupby("product_code", observed=True)
    df["prod_claim_count_prior"] = g.cumcount()
    df["prod_mean_amount_prior"] = (g["claim_amount_inr"]
                                    .apply(lambda s: s.shift(1).expanding().mean())
                                    .reset_index(level=0, drop=True))
    df["desc_len"] = df.description.str.split().str.len()
    df["days_since_purchase"] = (df.submitted_at - df.purchase_date).dt.days
    df["spec_version"] = spec_version
    out = path.replace("clean", f"features_{spec_version}")
    df.to_parquet(out)
    return out
```

Three things that make this a pipeline rather than a script: an **immutable dated snapshot**, so "the data" is a resolvable reference; **quarantine rather than silent dropping**, so you can inspect what broke; and **leakage-safe aggregates** built with `shift(1)` before any expanding window.

##### Baseline first, always

```python
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report

baseline = Pipeline([
    ("tfidf", TfidfVectorizer(ngram_range=(1, 2), min_df=3, max_features=60_000,
                              sublinear_tf=True)),
    ("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, class_weight="balanced", C=2.0)),
]).fit(train.description, train.category)

print(classification_report(test.category, baseline.predict(test.description),
                            digits=3, zero_division=0))
```

This takes twenty minutes and is the single most valuable number in the project. It establishes the bar every subsequent model must clear, and it frequently gets uncomfortably close to a transformer's performance — which is itself an important finding to report honestly. A capstone that says "the fine-tuned model beat TF-IDF by 6 macro-F1 points, at 40× the inference cost" is more credible than one that never checked.

##### The core model, tracked properly

```python
import mlflow, numpy as np
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForSequenceClassification, TrainingArguments, Trainer

mlflow.set_experiment("/capstone/claim-triage")

with mlflow.start_run(run_name=f"xlmr-{SPEC_VERSION}-{TRIAL}") as run:
    mlflow.set_tags({"git_sha": git_sha(), "data_snapshot": snapshot_uri,
                     "data_sha256": data_hash, "purpose": "candidate",
                     "spec_version": SPEC_VERSION})
    mlflow.log_params(cfg)

    tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("xlm-roberta-base")
    model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(
        "xlm-roberta-base", num_labels=len(CATEGORIES),
        id2label=ID2LABEL, label2id=LABEL2ID)

    trainer = Trainer(model=model, args=TrainingArguments(
        output_dir="out", num_train_epochs=4, learning_rate=2e-5,
        per_device_train_batch_size=16, gradient_accumulation_steps=2,
        warmup_ratio=0.06, weight_decay=0.01, bf16=True,
        eval_strategy="epoch", save_strategy="epoch",
        load_best_model_at_end=True, metric_for_best_model="macro_f1",
        seed=42,
    ), train_dataset=train_ds, eval_dataset=val_ds, compute_metrics=metrics_fn)
    trainer.train()

    # Evaluate on slices, with bootstrap confidence intervals
    report = evaluate_full(model, test_ds)
    mlflow.log_metrics({"macro_f1": report["macro_f1"],
                        "worst_category_precision": report["worst_precision"],
                        "p95_latency_ms": report["p95_latency_ms"]})
    for cat, f1 in report["per_category_f1"].items():
        mlflow.log_metric(f"f1__{cat}", f1)
    for region, f1 in report["per_region_f1"].items():
        mlflow.log_metric(f"f1__region_{region}", f1)

    mlflow.log_dict(report, "evaluation_report.json")
    mlflow.log_dict(provenance(), "provenance.json")
    mlflow.log_artifact("model_card.yaml")
    mlflow.transformers.log_model({"model": model, "tokenizer": tok}, "model")
```

Logging **latency alongside accuracy** at training time is a small habit with outsized signalling value — it says you think about deployment while you model.

##### Evaluation that survives scrutiny

Go beyond a single number:

- **Temporal holdout**, never a random split, if there is any time dimension.
- **Per-slice metrics** — by category, region, language, claim size. Report the worst slice prominently.
- **Bootstrap confidence intervals**, so a 3-point difference on 200 samples is not oversold.
- **Manual error review.** Read 100 misclassifications and taxonomise them. This is the highest-information-per-hour activity in the whole project, and the resulting table — "34% are genuine label errors, 28% are two categories that overlap by policy, 21% are OCR failures" — is what interviewers remember.
- **The gold set.** Where your labels are known to be noisy (risk R1), hand-label a few hundred and report against both.

```python
from sklearn.utils import resample

def bootstrap_ci(y_true, y_pred, metric_fn, n=1000, alpha=0.05):
    scores = []
    idx = np.arange(len(y_true))
    for _ in range(n):
        s = resample(idx)
        scores.append(metric_fn(y_true[s], y_pred[s]))
    return (float(np.percentile(scores, 100 * alpha / 2)),
            float(np.percentile(scores, 100 * (1 - alpha / 2))))
```

##### Reproducibility checklist

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Git SHA, clean tree] --> R[Reproducible run]
    B[Image digest / uv.lock] --> R
    C[Data snapshot + sha256] --> R
    D[Config file, no literals] --> R
    E[Seeds: python, numpy, torch] --> R
    R --> V{Rerun -> same metrics?}
    V -->|Yes| OK[Ship it]
    V -->|No| F[Find the unpinned thing]
```

Actually run the check: execute the pipeline twice with identical inputs and assert the metrics match to four decimal places. Teams that assume reproducibility rather than testing it are usually wrong, and finding out now is much cheaper than finding out during an audit.

##### Common mistakes

- Starting to code before writing the design document.
- No baseline, so no evidence the complex model was necessary.
- Random train/test split on temporal data.
- Reporting only an aggregate metric, hiding a collapsed category.
- Untracked experiments, so "the best model" cannot be reproduced.
- Building six shallow projects instead of one deep one.
- Clean benchmark data instead of messy real data.
- Silently dropping invalid rows instead of quarantining them.
- No manual error review, so the failure taxonomy is unknown.
- Scope creep turning a capstone into an unfinished platform.

##### Hands-on

Choose your project against the four criteria and write the full design document, including honest Non-goals and Risks sections. Build the data pipeline with immutable snapshots, schema validation with quarantine, PII redaction, and leakage-safe features. Establish a baseline within the first two days. Then build the core model with full MLflow tracking, and produce an evaluation report with per-slice metrics, bootstrap confidence intervals, and a taxonomised review of 100 errors.

For the mini-project deliverable, ship the complete Part 1 package: the design document, a reproducible data pipeline, a tracked and evaluated core model (or RAG/agent), a model card, and a `README` that a stranger can follow to reproduce your headline number from a clean checkout. Verify reproducibility by running it twice and comparing metrics. Tomorrow you deploy it — so leave the model behind a clean interface, and do not hard-code a single path.

##### Key takeaways

- One system taken to production depth beats six notebooks; interviews follow depth, not breadth.
- The design document's Non-goals and Risks sections are where judgement shows.
- Build the baseline first — it is the only evidence that your complex model earned its cost.
- Evaluate on temporal holdouts, per slice, with confidence intervals, and read 100 errors by hand.
- Pin code, environment, data, config and seeds — then actually test that a rerun reproduces the number.
